content: Pleurisy is a medical condition characterized by inflammation of the pleura, which is the membrane lining the pleural cavity surrounding the lungs. One of the hallmark symptoms of pleurisy, also referred to as pleuritis, is pleuritic chest pain. This type of pain is typically sharp and occurs during either inhalation or exhalation. The condition can arise from a variety of causes, both infectious and non-infectious in nature. The visceral pleura, which directly covers the lungs, lacks nociceptors or pain receptors. In contrast, the parietal pleura is innervated by somatic nerves that are capable of sensing pain. When the parietal pleura becomes inflamed, these somatic pain receptors are activated, leading to the characteristic pleuritic pain. Inflammation originating in the peripheral lung parenchyma can extend into the pleural space, involving the parietal pleura and triggering this pain response. The parietal pleura located along the outer rib cage and the lateral portions of each hemidiaphragm is innervated by intercostal nerves. Pain in these areas is typically localized to the skin regions supplied by these nerves. The central portion of each hemidiaphragm, however, is innervated by the phrenic nerve. When the phrenic nerve fibers are activated, the resulting pain is often referred to the ipsilateral neck or shoulder. Individuals with underlying lung diseases, such as pneumonia or tuberculosis, are at an increased risk of developing pleurisy. Early treatment of bacterial respiratory infections is an effective strategy to prevent the onset of pleurisy.
